[00:00:10] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for squeezing this in. we wanted to focus on throughput tuning for your private deployment, specifically the interplay between VPC pinning, pre-warming the KV cache and scheduler knobs.
[00:00:27] Liam: Yep, thanks. we, uh, we've been seeing tail latency blips when traffic bursts hit, and the cost math with our reserved nodes means we need high utilization.
[00:00:41] Daniel: Great, can you remind us of your traffic profile? p95 seq length, burstiness, arrival model?
[00:00:48] Sana: Sure—typical prompt lengths are 12 to 80 tokens, p95 ~ 220 tokens, p99 around 800 but those are rare; steady baseline RPS is 180, spikes to 1.2k during market opens, and most requests are single-turn.
[00:01:05] Daniel: Okay that explains why KV hit-rate drops during the opens—lots of new prefixes and cold KV entries.
[00:01:14] Marta: Quick note: on the private nodes you're using A100-s variant with 80GB and mixed-precision kernels. we saw mixed results moving to int4 on a 13B family; latency drops but generation artifacts increase slightly in some prompts.
[00:01:29] Liam: That's my big worry—quality regressions. we can't have hallucinations in trading summaries.
[00:01:36] Ava: Totally understood. today's goal is to find an operational compromise: maximize throughput with controlled token caps and KV prewarm so we reduce cold-start per-token cost but keep quality.
[00:01:48] 
[00:02:10] (discussion) Daniel walks through scheduler knobs and continuous batching model.
[00:02:15] Daniel: The scheduler has two knobs we usually tune together: the continuous batching window and max_num_seqs (we call it the per-GPU sequence cap). window is in ms and controls how long we wait to form a batch; lower window reduces latency but decreases packing efficiency. max_num_seqs sets how many concurrent sequences we allow in a scheduled batch chunk.
[00:02:40] Sana: Is max_num_seqs per-GPU or per-model?
[00:02:43] Daniel: Per-GPU. in Dedicated it maps to the number of sequences the runtime will accept to pack; in Private it's the same but you can pin GPUs via VPC placement to ensure predictable capacity.
[00:02:55] [00:03:00] Liam: about VPC pinning—we want to pin certain critical routes to a subset of nodes to guarantee throughput during market hours. what's the best practice?
[00:03:08] Marta: We recommend a two-tier pinning: reserve 20-30% of nodes for critical routes (low-latency SLOs) and leave the remainder for burstable workloads. use autoscaler burst policies for temporary overflow. also pin by model variant so you avoid packing incompatibilities.
[00:03:28] Daniel: One operational trick: set the scheduler to prefer packing shorter sequences into slots when load is mixed. that increases KV reuse because shorter sequences share prefixes more often.
[00:03:40] [00:03:58] (break / crosstalk)
[00:04:05] Sana: Can you explain KV prewarm? my team thought the KV cache was only populated during generation.
[00:04:12] Daniel: Right, by default KV is populated as inference runs; prewarm is a feature where we pre-seed KV cache for common prefixes or recent hot prompts. this reduces first-token latency and increases hit-rate during bursts. prewarm can be triggered by traffic heuristics or via an explicit upload in the private control plane.
[00:04:30] Liam: So we could pre-seed market-open templates?
[00:04:33] Daniel: Exactly. for BlueHarbor you could run a small job that runs through the 50 most common prefixes and warm the KV for those model variants right before market opens. that combined with pinning critical routes reduces the cold-token penalty.
[00:04:45] 
[00:05:10] Ava: Practical notes—prewarm costs some compute but often pays back quickly because it avoids high tail latencies and keeps throughput high. we model prewarm cost vs token saved in the Optimize tool.
[00:05:22] Liam: What's the recommended max_num_seqs for our hardware?
[00:05:26] Daniel: For A100-80GB with your 13B family at ~p95 seq=220 I'd start with max_num_seqs=32 for the critical pinned pool and 48 for the burst pool, then run throughput tests. lower it if you see latency tails caused by oversized packing and KV eviction.
[00:05:45] Priya: you said eviction—how do we avoid KV thrashing?
[00:05:48] Marta: Tune cache size and eviction policy. we expose a hotness window and TTL per entry. combine that with prewarm: when you prewarm the most common prefixes you effectively raise the hit-rate so eviction pressure drops. also watch for extremely long sequences (p99) which can push out many entries—apply token_limit soft caps to prevent single requests from starving the cache.
[00:06:10] [00:06:22] Evan: about token limits—can we apply per-route token caps and soft-fail vs hard-fail policies? security wants guaranteed resource isolation.
[00:06:29] Ava: Yes, Redwood supports per-route token_limit and soft cap policies. soft caps emit a warning and optionally apply compression strategies (e.g., summarize prompt preface) and can downgrade to a faster quantized path before hard-failing. Hard caps reject with 429/413 as configured.
[00:06:47] Sana: Summarization before sending measurable—we need to test for quality.
[00:06:50] Daniel: We typically add a small eval harness: run 1000 samples through quantized path and compare rouge/semantic-sim to baseline. For trading summaries we set a high quality threshold. if quantization fails quality, we fallback to float16 path automatically.
[00:07:06] 
[00:07:40] (Deep-dive on quantization and token throughput)
[00:07:42] Marta: Int8 generally gives you significant speedups with minimal degradation on many families; int4 is more aggressive and varies by prompt. On-prem with custom kernels might have different performance characteristics—ensure kernel selection is validated.
[00:07:55] Liam: can we toggle quantization per-route?
[00:07:56] Daniel: Yes, per-route model profiles allow you to specify quantized variant or dynamic fallback. so critical routes can pin to fp16 while lower-priority routes use int8/int4.
[00:08:08] [00:08:20] Ava: Let's talk a little about scheduler windows and latency SLOs. if you set the window to 8ms you'll get better p50 but suffer packing efficiency; set it to 25-40ms for high packing. for your workloads during market opens we recommend a dynamic window: 10ms during low traffic, expand to 30ms when throughput target is needed.
[00:08:42] Priya: Is dynamic windowing supported in private?
[00:08:44] Daniel: Yes, through runtime policies. you can base it on RPS or on latency percentiles. we've shipped a sample policy in the runbook I'll share.
[00:08:55] 
[00:09:15] (Performance tradeoff examples)
[00:09:20] Daniel: Example: with max_num_seqs=48 and window=30ms on your hardware, we measured tokens/sec about 2.6x of baseline fp16 single-stream, but p99 latency jumped during heavy prefix churn. Flip to max_num_seqs=32 + kv_prewarm and we saw p99 drop by 35% while tokens/sec reduced by 12%—better for SLOS.
[00:09:44] Sana: that's helpful. can you share the raw CSVs?
[00:09:47] Daniel: will share. action item.
[00:09:50] 
[00:10:30] (Mis-transcription / quick interruptions)
[00:10:33] Speaker 1: uh can you do a chart that shows cost per token vs p99?
[00:10:36] Ava: yes we'll include a cost curve with each configuration.
[00:10:39] 
[00:11:00] (Security tangent) Evan: encryption—if we run private in our VPC and use customer KMS, how is key management handled? do you support HSM-backed keys?
[00:11:10] Marta: We integrate with customer KMS and can support HSM via standard KMS providers. audit logs for each inference request are captured and stored in your logging endpoint. we'll provide mapping for request_id -> model_version for audits.
[00:11:22] Evan: good. also need SSO and RBAC mapping for the console.
[00:11:26] Ava: yes, SAML + SCIM currently supported; we'll include the guide in the security pack.
[00:11:31] 
[00:12:05] (Bench discussion)
[00:12:10] Daniel: Next practical step: we propose 3 bench runs in your staging VPC: 1) baseline fp16, max_num_seqs=24, window=15ms; 2) kv_prewarm + max_num_seqs=32 + window=30ms; 3) kv_prewarm + quantized int8 + max_num_seqs=48 + window=30ms. capture p50/p95/p99 tokens/sec, KV hit rate, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens. run for 60 minutes each to get stable metrics.
[00:12:38] Liam: ok, we can schedule that over the next week.
[00:12:40] 
[00:13:00] (QA, misc)
[00:13:05] Sana: what's the impact of long sequences on the scheduler?
[00:13:08] Daniel: Long sequences occupy a sequence slot for many steps; they can reduce packing and cause eviction. mitigation: token_limit per-route or pre-sample and chunk long sequences into segments with KV checkpointing.
[00:13:22] Priya: chunking implications for context?
[00:13:25] Daniel: you need to preserve KV across segments; our runtime supports checkpointing KV to avoid recomputing from scratch. that's what we do for long form generation.
[00:13:35] 
[00:14:00] (Wrap up)
[00:14:05] Ava: quick recap: 1) we'll share VPC runbook and dynamic-window policy, 2) Daniel will run and share bench CSVs, 3) Liam will provide traces, 4) Evan will confirm KMS and security contacts.
[00:14:22] Liam: sounds good. any outstanding blockers?
[00:14:25] Evan: none on security beyond confirming KMS.
[00:14:28] Ava: great. thanks everyone.
[00:14:30] (call ends)
